title: Lost and Found, Honest Weights, Fair Wages
bigQuestion: How does the Talmud try to make everyday trades, finds and jobs fair for everyone?

story.title: One Coat, Two Hands
story.kicker: Two students grab the same coat at the same moment, and a very old book has a plan for that.
paragraphs: It was the last day before winter break at a school in Chicago. The lost-and-found box sat by the door. Maya reached in for a blue coat. Jonah reached in at the same second. Both hands closed on the collar. "It's mine," said Maya. "It's mine," said Jonah. Neither one let go.

Ms. Feld did not take a side. She went to her shelf and pulled down a thick book. "This is a tractate of the Talmud called *Bava Metzia*," she said. "The name means 'the middle gate.' It is about things people find, buy, borrow and lend. And it starts with exactly your problem."

She read the first Mishnah in her own words. Two people are holding one coat. Each says, "I found it." Each says, "It is all mine." The rabbis' answer: each one promises they own at least half. Then they split it. Jonah frowned. "Cut the coat?" "No," said Ms. Feld. "Sell it, and share the money. Or share what it is worth."

"But what if only one of us is telling the truth?" asked Maya. Ms. Feld smiled. "The rabbis asked that too. They asked for pages and pages. That is what the Talmud is: a long, careful argument about being fair." Maya and Jonah looked at the coat. Then they both let go and checked the name tag inside.
story.think: Why might splitting the coat be fairer than letting the faster or stronger person keep it?

lessons.title: Three Gates About Fairness
lessons.mainIdea: Bava Metzia, the middle gate, is one of three tractates about damages, property and fair dealing.
reading: The *Mishnah* is the older, shorter part of the Talmud. Rabbinic tradition says Rabbi Judah the Prince arranged it, around 200 CE. It has six big parts called orders. One order is called Nezikin. The word means 'damages.' It is about harm, money, courts and fairness.

Three of its tractates are called gates. A *tractate* is one book of the Mishnah. Bava Kamma is 'the first gate.' Bava Metzia is 'the middle gate.' Bava Batra is 'the last gate.' Long ago they were one very long book. Later they were split into three parts.

Bava Metzia is about everyday things. What do you do with a lost wallet? What is a fair price? When do you pay a worker? The Gemara, the later discussion, asks questions about each rule. This chapter follows those questions.

words.d: the older, shorter core of the Talmud, a set of rulings arranged around 200 CE
one book of the Mishnah or Talmud, about one set of topics
the order of the Mishnah about damages, property, courts and fair dealing

look.title: The Three Gates
look.cite: Mishnah, order Nezikin; chapter counts as printed in standard editions
look.prompt: The three gates have the same number of chapters. What might that tell you about how they were once one book?

check.q: What does the name Bava Metzia mean?
check.why: Bava Metzia means 'the middle gate.' It sits between Bava Kamma, the first gate, and Bava Batra, the last gate.

check.q: Which order of the Mishnah holds the three gates?
check.why: Nezikin means 'damages.' It is the order about harm, money, courts and fair dealing.

check.q: Which of these is a topic of Bava Metzia?
check.why: Bava Metzia is about things people find, buy, borrow and lend. Lost objects are in its second chapter.

lessons.title: Two Hold One Coat
lessons.mainIdea: The tractate opens with two people holding one garment, and the rabbis' first answer is: promise, then share.
reading: The first Mishnah of Bava Metzia is short. Two people are holding one *tallit*, a cloak or coat. One says, "I found it." The other says, "I found it." Each one says the whole thing is theirs. The Mishnah rules that each one takes an *oath*. Each swears they own no less than half. Then they divide it.

Why an oath? The *Gemara* asks this right away. It gives an answer. If people could just grab and claim, some would grab what is not theirs. A serious promise makes a person stop and think. The Gemara then asks more questions. What if one says it is all his, and the other says only half is his? The Mishnah has an answer for that too.

Readers of the Talmud love this opening. Rashi, a teacher in France about 1,000 years ago, explains each word. Later rabbis wrote whole books on this one page. For the course, notice two things. The rule protects both people. And the rabbis keep asking 'but what if?' That is the way the whole Talmud moves.

words.d: a cloak or garment; in the first Mishnah of Bava Metzia, the thing two people both hold
a very serious promise that something is true
the later discussion of the Mishnah, written in Aramaic and Hebrew

look.title: The First Mishnah, in Plain Words
look.text: Two people are holding a garment. One says, 'I found it,' and the other says, 'I found it.' One says, 'All of it is mine,' and the other says, 'All of it is mine.' Each one swears that he owns no less than half of it, and they divide it.
look.cite: Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1, retold in plain words; compare Michael L. Rodkinson, Babylonian Talmud, 1896–1903
look.prompt: Why do you think the rabbis asked for a promise before the two people share the garment?

check.q: In the first Mishnah of Bava Metzia, what do the two people both say?
check.why: Both people say, 'I found it,' and both claim the whole garment. That is what makes the case hard.

check.q: What does the Mishnah tell the two people to do?
choices: Give it to a judge to keep
Take an oath, then divide it
check.why: Each one swears they own at least half, and then they divide the garment's value.

check.q: What does the Gemara do with the Mishnah's rule?
choices: It copies it with no comment
It asks why and adds harder cases
It turns it into a song
check.why: The Gemara asks why an oath is needed and then tests the rule with new 'what if' cases.

lessons.title: Bring It Back
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah tells a finder to return a lost animal or object, and the rabbis built a whole set of rules on that verse.
reading: The rules about lost things start in the Torah. In Deuteronomy, the fifth book, there is a command. If you see your neighbor's ox or sheep wandering, do not look away. Bring it back. The same goes for a coat or anything lost. Jewish tradition calls this *hashavat aveidah*, returning a lost object.

The second chapter of Bava Metzia takes that verse and asks questions. What counts as lost? What if you do not know whose it is? What if it is a live animal that needs feeding? Do you have to pick up something dirty? The rabbis answer each one. The verse says 'do not hide yourself.' So a person may not pretend they did not see.

The Gemara also protects the finder. If returning a thing would cost the finder more than it is worth, the rules change. An old, honored person is not made to carry a heavy sack through the street. The law asks for kindness, but it is a fair kind of kindness.

words.d: returning a lost object; the rabbis' name for the rule in Deuteronomy 22
the fifth book of the Torah; it holds the verses about lost things and paying workers

look.title: The Verse the Rabbis Start From
look.text: Thou shalt not see thy brother's ox or his sheep driven away, and hide thyself from them; thou shalt surely bring them back unto thy brother.
look.prompt: What two things does this verse say not to do, and what one thing does it say to do?

check.q: Which book of the Torah holds the rule about returning a lost ox or sheep?
check.why: Deuteronomy 22:1–3 tells a person to bring back a neighbor's lost animal or object.

check.q: What does 'hide thyself' mean in the verse?
choices: Pretend you did not see it
check.why: The rabbis read 'hide thyself' as looking away and pretending not to see a lost thing.

check.q: Which case shows the Gemara protecting the finder too?
choices: A finder must carry any load, no matter what
An honored elder is not made to carry a heavy sack
check.why: The Gemara says an elder who would never carry such a load is not forced to; the rule is fair to finders also.

lessons.title: A Sign Tells Whose
lessons.mainIdea: A found thing with a sign is announced; a found thing with no sign, like loose coins, belongs to the finder.
reading: How can a finder know who lost a thing? The Mishnah's answer is the *siman*, a sign. A sign is a mark that only the owner would know. A purse with coins in it has a sign. The owner can say how many coins, or what the purse looks like. Fruit in a basket has a sign: the basket.

Some things have no sign. The Mishnah lists them. Scattered coins in the street. Scattered fruit on the road. A baker's loaves, which all look the same. Loose bundles of grain. No one could prove such a thing was theirs. So the Mishnah says the finder may keep it.

When a thing has a sign, the finder must *announce* it. In Temple times there was a special stone in Jerusalem. Finders stood on it and called out what they found. Someone who lost a thing came and gave the sign. If the sign matched, they got it back. The Mishnah says the loser gives the sign. The finder does not tell it first.

words.d: a sign or mark on a lost thing that only its owner would know
to tell people in public that something was found

look.title: Sign or No Sign?
look.text: Here are four things a person might find on the way to school: a backpack with a name inside; three loose quarters on the sidewalk; one apple rolling on the road; a lunchbox with a sticker and a note. Sort them into two groups: things with a sign, and things with no sign.
look.prompt: For each thing, say why it is in its group. Which ones would the Mishnah say to announce?

check.q: What is a siman?
choices: A sign only the owner would know
check.why: A siman is a sign or mark that shows who the owner is, like the number of coins in a purse.

check.q: Which found thing does the Mishnah say the finder may keep?
choices: A purse with coins in it
check.why: Scattered coins have no sign, so no owner could prove they were theirs. The Mishnah lets the finder keep them.

check.q: Who gives the sign, according to the Mishnah?
choices: The finder tells the sign first
The person who lost the thing
Both must say it at once
check.why: The loser describes the sign. If the finder told it first, anyone could repeat it and claim the thing.

lessons.title: When the Owner Gives Up
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara asks whether an owner who gave up hope still owns the lost thing, and Abaye and Rava disagree.
reading: The rabbis had a word for giving up: *ye'ush*. Say a coin falls into a river. The owner sighs and says, 'It is gone.' Rabbinic tradition holds that the owner has let it go. A finder who pulls it out later may keep it. The owner gave up hope, so the coin is no longer theirs.

Now comes a harder case. What if the owner does not even know the thing is lost yet? Two famous teachers argued about it. They were *Abaye* and *Rava*, who lived in Babylonia around 300 to 350 CE. Abaye said: no. The owner has not given up, because they do not know. Rava said: the owner would give up if they knew. So it counts already.

The Gemara records both views. Later tradition follows Abaye here. This is one of only six cases where the law follows Abaye over Rava. But the point for us is the way the argument goes. Each side brings proofs. Each side answers the other. Both voices stay on the page.

words.d: giving up hope of getting a lost thing back
a Babylonian rabbi of the 300s CE; his debates with Rava fill the Talmud
a Babylonian rabbi of the 300s CE, Abaye's study partner and rival

look.title: Abaye and Rava on Giving Up
look.text: The Gemara asks about giving up without knowing. Abaye says it does not count: the owner has not given up, because he does not yet know the thing is lost. Rava says it does count: once he knows, he will surely give up, so we treat it as given up now.
look.cite: Bava Metzia 21b, paraphrased; compare the William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria
look.prompt: Which side would you argue for, and what is one reason the other side might give?

check.q: What does ye'ush mean?
choices: Giving up hope of getting it back
check.why: Ye'ush is the owner giving up hope. After ye'ush, the rabbis hold, the finder may keep the thing.

check.q: Abaye and Rava lived in which place?
check.why: Abaye and Rava taught in Babylonia in the 300s CE. Their debates are all through the Gemara.

check.q: In the case of giving up without knowing, what did Abaye say?
choices: It counts, because the owner will give up later
It does not count, because the owner does not know yet
The coin goes to the court
check.why: Abaye said an owner cannot give up on something they do not know is lost. Rava took the other side.

lessons.title: Just Weights and Measures
lessons.mainIdea: Leviticus commands honest scales, and the Mishnah adds rules for keeping measuring tools clean and true.
reading: Long before there were price tags, people bought by weight. A seller put a stone on one side of a *scale*. Grain or oil went on the other side. A cheating seller could use a light stone or a bent scale. The Torah speaks to this. Leviticus says to keep honest scales, honest weights and honest measures.

The Mishnah turns the verse into daily rules. In Bava Batra, the last gate, it says a seller must clean their measures. Sticky oil or wet flour can stick to a cup. Then the buyer gets less. So a wholesaler cleans the measures once a month. A shopkeeper cleans them twice a week. The scale is wiped after every weighing.

The Gemara adds a strong warning. It says a person may not even keep a false weight in the house. Not to use it, just to have it. Why? A false weight is a temptation. Jewish tradition reads this as a rule about trust. If buyers cannot trust the scale, the whole market breaks.

words.d: a tool with two sides for weighing; a seller uses it to measure out goods
the third book of the Torah; it holds the verse about honest weights

look.title: Honest Scales in the Torah
look.text: Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.
look.prompt: An ephah measures dry things and a hin measures liquids. Why might the verse name both?

check.q: Which book of the Torah commands honest weights and measures?
check.why: Leviticus 19:35–36 tells people to keep just balances, weights and measures.

check.q: Why does the Mishnah say to clean measuring cups?
choices: So the rabbi can bless them
So sticky leftovers do not shortchange the buyer
check.why: Mishnah Bava Batra 5:10 says sticky flour or oil in a cup means the buyer gets less.

check.q: What does the Gemara say about keeping a false weight at home?
choices: It is fine if you never use it
You may not even keep one
check.why: The Gemara, in Bava Batra 89b, says a person may not keep a false weight at all, because it tempts.

lessons.title: No Overcharging
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah calls charging far too much ona'ah, wronging, and sets a clear line: one-sixth over the price.
reading: Sellers set prices. But the Mishnah says there is a limit. Charging much more than a thing is worth is called *ona'ah*. The word means 'wronging' or 'overreaching.' The Torah says in Leviticus, 'You shall not wrong one another.' Rabbinic tradition reads that as a rule about prices.

How much is too much? The Mishnah gives a number. If the price is off by one-sixth, that is ona'ah. The Mishnah uses coins of its day. A *sela* was worth 24 small coins called ma'ah. Four ma'ah over on a sela is one-sixth. At that point the buyer may ask for the extra back. If it is even more, the buyer may cancel the sale.

The rule cuts both ways. A buyer who pays far too little has wronged the seller. The Mishnah protects the person who did not know the price. Historians point out that markets in the Roman world often had no fixed prices. So this was a real protection. It gave a shopper a way to complain.

words.d: wronging someone, in money or in words; charging far too much is ona'ah
a silver coin in the time of the Mishnah, worth 24 ma'ah

look.title: Coins in the Mishnah's Example
rows: Extra ma'ah on a sela that counts as ona'ah
look.cite: Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:3, standard coin values as the Mishnah uses them
look.prompt: Four out of 24 is one-sixth. If a fair price today is 12 dollars, how many extra dollars would be one-sixth?

check.q: What does ona'ah mean?
check.why: Ona'ah means wronging. The Mishnah uses it for unfair prices and, later, for hurtful words.

check.q: How far off must a price be for the Mishnah to call it ona'ah?
check.why: Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:3 sets the line at one-sixth, four ma'ah on a sela of 24.

check.q: Who does the ona'ah rule protect?
check.why: A buyer who is overcharged is wronged, and a seller who is underpaid is wronged too.

lessons.title: Hurting With Words
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah says words can wrong a person as much as money can, and the Gemara says even more.
reading: The same Mishnah chapter takes a surprising turn. After prices, it talks about words. Just as there is ona'ah in buying and selling, it says, there is ona'ah in words. The Mishnah gives examples. Do not ask a seller 'how much is this?' if you have no plan to buy. That raises a hope and drops it.

The Mishnah goes on. If a person has changed their ways, do not say, 'Remember what you used to do.' If someone joined the Jewish people from another family, do not bring up their past. Those words hurt. The Gemara adds that shaming a person in public is very serious. It compares the face going pale to a kind of bloodshed.

Then the Gemara compares the two kinds of wronging. Which is worse, money or words? It says words are worse. Why? Money can be given back. A hurtful word cannot be taken back. The Talmud does not just care about fair prices. It cares about a person's *dignity*, their sense of worth.

words.d: wronging with words; hurting someone with what you say
a person's worth and self-respect

look.title: Money or Words?
look.text: Two things happened at the school store. First, Sam was charged two dollars too much for a notebook. Second, a classmate laughed at Sam in front of the line and said, 'You can't even count money.' The Gemara in Bava Metzia says one of these is worse than the other.
look.prompt: Which one does the Gemara say is worse, and what reason does it give? Do you agree?

check.q: Which of these is an example of ona'at devarim from the Mishnah?
choices: Asking a price with no plan to buy
check.why: Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 says asking 'how much?' with no plan to buy is wronging with words.

check.q: Why does the Gemara say wronging with words is worse than with money?
choices: Money can be given back, but words cannot
check.why: Bava Metzia 58b says money can be returned, but a hurtful word cannot be taken back.

check.q: What does the Gemara compare public shaming to?
check.why: The Gemara notes the face going pale and treats public shaming as very close to shedding blood.

lessons.title: Pay Before the Sun Sets
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says pay a hired worker the same day, and the Mishnah spells out when day and night workers are paid.
reading: Many people in the time of the Mishnah worked by the day. A farmer hired helpers for the harvest. A builder hired carriers. Such a worker needed the money that night to buy food. The Torah knew this. Deuteronomy says: pay him the same day, before the sun goes down, for he is poor and counts on it.

The Mishnah in Bava Metzia makes it exact. A worker hired for the day is paid any time that night. A worker hired for the night is paid any time the next day. A worker hired by the week or the month is paid when the job ends. If the employer holds back pay past that time, the Mishnah says he breaks a Torah rule.

The Mishnah also protects the *employer*, the person who hires. If the worker never asked for pay, the employer has not broken the rule. If the employer handed the pay to a shopkeeper to give the worker, he is not to blame. The rule is not meant to trap anyone. It is meant to get a poor worker fed tonight.

words.d: a person paid by the day, night, week or month for their labor
the person who hires and pays a worker

look.title: The Same Day
look.text: In the same day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it: lest he cry against thee unto the LORD and it be sin in thee.
look.prompt: What reason does the verse give for paying the same day? Who is the verse worried about?

check.q: When must a worker hired for the day be paid, says the Mishnah?
choices: Only at the end of the month
check.why: Mishnah Bava Metzia 9:11 says a day worker collects any time during the following night.

check.q: What reason does Deuteronomy 24:15 give for same-day pay?
choices: The worker is poor and counts on it
check.why: The verse says the worker is poor and sets his heart on the pay, so it must not wait.

check.q: When is an employer NOT to blame for late pay, says the Mishnah?
choices: When the worker did not ask for it
check.why: The Mishnah says if the worker never asked, the employer has not broken the rule of same-day pay.

lessons.title: The Broken Barrels
lessons.mainIdea: A story in Bava Metzia shows a rabbi telling an employer to go beyond the strict law and treat his workers with mercy.
reading: The Gemara tells a story. A man named Rabbah bar bar Chanan hired porters to move barrels of wine. They dropped the barrels, and the wine spilled. He was angry. He took their cloaks as payment for the loss. The porters went to Rav, the great teacher of Babylonia. Rav told the man: give back the cloaks.

The man asked, 'Is that the law?' Rav quoted a verse from Proverbs: 'that you may walk in the way of good men.' He gave back the cloaks. Then the porters said, 'We are poor. We worked all day. We have nothing to eat.' Rav said: pay them their wages. The man asked again, 'Is that the law?' Rav quoted the rest of the verse: 'and keep the paths of the righteous.'

Readers have argued about this story for centuries. Some say Rav found a real rule here. Others say Rav was asking a scholar to go beyond the rule. Jewish tradition has a name for that: *lifnim mishurat hadin*, inside the line of the law. This chapter began with an argument over a coat. It ends with mercy for hungry workers. The Talmud holds both.

words.d: a leading rabbi who brought Mishnah study to Babylonia in the 200s CE
going beyond the strict letter of the law to do what is kind
a worker who carries heavy loads for pay

look.title: Two Ways to Read Rav
look.text: Reading one: Rav was stating the law. Porters who drop a barrel by accident do not owe for it, so the man had to return the cloaks and pay. Reading two: Rav was asking for more than the law. The man was a scholar, and Rav wanted him to act with extra kindness. Both readings come from the same page, Bava Metzia 83a.
look.prompt: Which reading fits the man's question, 'Is that the law?' better? What clue in the story do you use?

check.q: What did Rabbah bar bar Chanan take from the porters?
check.why: After the wine spilled, he took the porters' cloaks. Rav told him to give them back.

check.q: Which book did Rav quote to the employer?
check.why: Rav quoted Proverbs 2:20, 'that thou mayest walk in the way of good men.'

check.q: What does lifnim mishurat hadin mean?
choices: Going beyond the strict law to be kind
check.why: Lifnim mishurat hadin means acting inside, or beyond, the line the law draws, out of kindness.

review.q: What does Bava Metzia mean, and what is it about?
choices: 'The middle gate'; things people find, buy, borrow and lend
review.why: Bava Metzia is 'the middle gate,' the tractate about everyday dealings: finds, sales, loans and wages.

review.q: In the coat case, what happens after the two people take an oath?
review.why: Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1: each swears to at least half, and they divide it.

review.q: A finder picks up a purse with seven coins inside. What does the Mishnah say to do?
choices: Keep it, since coins have no sign
Announce it, since the purse and count are a sign
review.why: Money in a purse has a sign, the purse and the number. Things with a sign must be announced.

review.q: Who argued that giving up without knowing does not count?
review.why: Abaye said an owner who does not know the thing is lost has not given up. Rava disagreed.

review.q: Which verse do the rabbis use for honest scales?
review.why: Leviticus 19:36 commands just balances, just weights and just measures.

review.q: A seller charges one-sixth more than a fair price. What does the Mishnah call this?
review.why: Overcharging by one-sixth is ona'ah, wronging, in Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:3.

review.q: Why does Deuteronomy say to pay a worker before sunset?
choices: Because the worker is poor and counts on the pay
Because coins are hard to see in the dark
review.why: Deuteronomy 24:15 says the worker is poor and sets his heart on the wages.

review.q: In the story of the broken barrels, what did Rav tell the employer to do?
choices: Return the cloaks and pay the porters
review.why: Bava Metzia 83a: Rav told him to give back the cloaks and then to pay the hungry porters.
